1.title: Pinot Gris: From Tokay d'Alsace to Today's Name
1.html:
Pinot Gris was long called "Tokay d'Alsace" or "Tokay-Pinot Gris" and is the grey-skinned mutation of Pinot Noir (named for its berry colour). The name "Tokay" easily suggests a link with Hungary's Tokaji sweet wines, but there is in fact no connection.

EU rules in 1984 formally allowed the name "Tokay Pinot Gris", but under an agreement reached in 1993 between Alsace, Hungary and the EU, from the 2007 vintage the name Tokay passed into history and the variety is simply called Pinot Gris.

An early-ripening variety with unstable yields; the berries are grey-blue to bluish grey. It can be used for Grand Cru, VT and SGN, and currently covers 14% of plantings.
2.title: Wine Style of Pinot Gris
2.html:
Style: opulent, full, round and rich — the Alsace white with the fullest, heaviest body (the most capiteux), yet it still keeps a pleasing acidity balance; the aromas are fresh and abundant, more restrained than Alsace wines with terpenic notes (such as Muscat). Pinot Gris from good vintages has excellent ageing potential.

Because it pairs with such a wide range of dishes — from raw seafood to truffle dishes, from noble-rot desserts to poultry — Pinot Gris holds an important place on wine lists in Alsace (and around the world).
3.title: Muscat: The Driest and Most Exuberant Aromatic Variety
3.html:
Muscat has been recorded in Alsace since 1510, coming from the East, and two varieties are grown today:

Muscat "dit d'Alsace" (small-berried white / pink Muscat): the same as the Muscat of southern France, relatively late-ripening in the Rhine climate, and gradually being replaced by Muscat Ottonel, which is more refined and has a wild aromatic character.
Muscat Ottonel: origin unknown (on the market in France since 1852), with Chasselas thought to be one parent; it ripens earlier, with a fine skin and delicate muscat flavour.

Both can be used for Grand Cru, VT and SGN. They now cover only 2.25% of plantings, the rarest of the "four noble white varieties".
4.title: Wine Style of Muscat
4.html:
Style: fresh and light — the driest and lightest-bodied of Alsace's top wines, yet with an exuberant, intense grape aroma, as if the taste of the grape itself had been captured in the wine, which makes it especially suited as a light aperitif.

Classic pairings include asparagus and lightly spiced dishes; you can even try foie gras or exotic cuisine (Chinese, Mexican, Pakistani), where the spices set off its exuberant aroma. It is best drunk young and fresh to enjoy its delicate fruity vitality.
5.question: What is distinctive about Alsace Muscat among the "four noble white varieties" (Riesling / Gewurztraminer / Pinot Gris / Muscat)?
5.options.0: It is the only variety allowed to be chaptalised
5.options.1: It is the driest and lightest-bodied, yet has the most exuberant grape aroma, ideal as an aperitif
5.options.2: It is the only variety that cannot be used for VT / SGN
5.options.3: It is the most widely planted variety
5.explanation: Muscat is the driest and lightest-bodied of Alsace's "four noble white varieties", yet has an especially exuberant, intense grape aroma — as if the flavour of the grape itself were captured in the wine — which makes it especially suited as a light aperitif. It now covers only 2.25% of plantings, the rarest of the four.
